h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר ט׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Tes

p: בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי (שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב הֲלָכָה ג ט, ב)
and in the Midrash Tanchuma (Ki Sisa 10)
that the shekalim atone for the sin of the Calf,
for their having sold Rachel's firstborn;
the root is the blemish of the serpent,
וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּתְחַבֵּר לָהּ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
and through Adam HaRishon's joining with her
the filth was brought into Adam HaRishon and his seed,
the blemish of the hundred and thirty years
which is the blemish of the sale of Yosef,
And at the time of Matan Torah
the entire corruption of the serpent was rectified,
and they would not have died,
as before the corruption of the serpent;
So too the sin of the Calf
"On the day I make account, I will bring to account";
and so the sin of the sale of Yosef
הָיָה שָׁמוּר עַד עֲשָׂרָה הֲרוּגֵי מַלְכוּת
was kept until the Ten Martyrs,
as they said in the Zohar Chadash (end of Eichah).
וּשְׁנֵיהֶם נִדְרְשׁוּ בַּזֹּהַר חָדָשׁ כִּי תִשָּׂא
Both are expounded in the Zohar Chadash on Ki Sisa
וּבְרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת כִּי תִשָּׂא
And in the Ra'aya Meheimna at the start of Parshas Ki Sisa
[זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ חֵלֶק ב קפז, ב] אִיתָא
he shall not go beyond ten, etc.;
"and the poor" — this is the Tzaddik —
"shall not give less" than ten, etc.
is Kudsha Brich Hu, as is known,
But the matter is as we said:
that is, in the aspect of the Middle Pillar.
And there is "one who passes among those counted,"
as they said in the Zohar Chadash
And about this it says "the rich" —
in the aspect of the Middle Pillar,
"shall not give more" than the yud.
And "the poor," who rectifies only the attribute of Tzaddik,
"shall not give less" than the yud.
And he cites (in the Ra'aya Meheimna ibid.)
and "shall not give less," as it is said,
and they explained it as referring to the attribute of Daas.
so that even the galbanum gives off a good scent,
and that is through supernal teshuvah,
in the manner of what is said (Mishlei 2:5),
"Then you will understand the fear of Hashem
and find the knowledge of G-d" —
that is, he merits the attainment of Daas;
and knowledge is pleasant to your soul" —
into the depth of the heart's understanding,
and he might think that there are eleven lights;
עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר הֶעָשִׁיר לֹא יַרְבֶּה
about this it says, "the rich shall not give more":
for since his willful sins become for him like merits,
as it says, "on account of them he shall live,"
it is included in the ten,
just as Daas is included in the ten attributes
and fills the place of Keser.
And "the poor" is the Tzaddik, as mentioned above,
who does not merit the aspect of Daas,
and he might think that since the first attribute
and one has no grasp of it whatsoever,
which He emanated for the creation of the world
so that they could be grasped;
עַל זֶה אָמַר לֹא יַמְעִיט מֵעֶשֶׂר
about this it says, "shall not give less" than ten,
כְּמָה דְּאַתְּ אָמַר עֶשֶׂר וְלֹא תֵּשַׁע
as it is said, "ten and not nine" —
that one merits the lower Chochmah,
and it is also from the dew of Atika —
the dew of Torah revives them,
as they said in the Tikkunei Zohar

paragraphs.text: Shabbos 146a — “When the serpent came upon Chavah, it cast impurity into her. Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai, had their impurity cease; the nations, who did not stand at Mount Sinai, did not have their impurity cease. Rav Acha son of Rava asked Rav Ashi: What of converts? He answered: Though they themselves were not there, their heavenly counterparts were present, as it is written, ‘With those who stand here with us today before Hashem our God, and with those who are not here with us today.’”

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 18b — “Rabbi Yirmiyah ben Elazar said: During all the years that Adam was under a ban he begot spirits, demons and lilin, as it says, ‘Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot in his likeness, after his image’—implying that until then he had not begotten after his image. Rabbi Meir said: Adam was greatly pious. When he saw that death had been decreed through him, he fasted for one hundred and thirty years, separated from his wife for one hundred and thirty years, and wore a belt of fig branches for one hundred and thirty years.” The Gemara reconciles the accounts by explaining that the former refers to involuntary emission. Its description of the 130 years is the background here; the connection with the sale of Yosef is Rav Tzadok’s further interpretation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 15 — “‘Yaakov sought to dwell in tranquility; the anger of Yosef sprang upon him’: these are the corruptions of the bris. That is the matter of the sale of Yosef, the level of tzaddik yesod olam, as a slave among the nations.” Rav Tzadok there identifies the sale of Yosef as a flaw in yesod, which is why it can share one root with Adam’s 130-year flaw and with the Calf.

paragraphs.text: Avodah Zarah 5a, on Tehillim 82:6–7 — “Rabbi Yosei says: Israel accepted the Torah only so that the Angel of Death would have no dominion over them, as it is written, ‘I said: You are divine beings, and all of you sons of the Most High.’ You damaged your deeds: ‘Indeed, like Adam you shall die.’” This is Rabbi Yosei’s position in the Gemara’s discussion; the Sages give a different explanation of the Torah’s removal of subjection. Rav Tzadok follows the position that relates the calf to the return of death.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Rashi on Shemos 32:34, s.v. Uveyom pokdi — “‘On the day I make an accounting’: Now I have listened to you and refrained from destroying them together. Yet whenever I make an accounting of their sins, I will also account against them a little of this sin together with the other sins. No calamity comes upon Israel without some repayment of the sin of the calf.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Rashi makes explicit the continuing character of the calf’s consequence. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok places it beside the sale of Yosef as an injury whose charge reappears in later generations; the two episodes need not have the same historical punishment to share that structural feature.

paragraphs.text: Zohar Chadash, end of Midrash HaNe’elam on Eichah, paragraphs 105–116 — “The serpent stood and demanded judgment, invoking ‘One who steals a person and sells him.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, answered the serpent: Yosef was not yet an adult man, and he was not found in their possession. It returned and cited the other verse, ‘If a man is found stealing a person from among his brothers.’ For eight hundred years that serpent stood demanding judgment. Then it descended, confounded the world, and put this spirit into the wicked king of Rome, who demanded judgment from the mighty ones of the world. Woe for this, woe for the world: such a distortion of judgment had not been found since the world was created.” The ensuing lament describes ten radiant souls departing Gan Eden and explicitly asks why a charge remained after Yosef had forgiven his brothers. It portrays the catastrophe as the serpent’s accusation and a grievous distortion during the Mother’s exile, rather than a simple legal equation that ignores forgiveness.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sefas Emes, Pekudei–Shekalim 5649 (1889) — “Concerning ‘The rich shall not increase’: The gold and copper donated to the Mishkan followed each individual’s generosity, but the counted silver was equal. This shows that the love and desire in Israel’s hearts are the power Hashem planted within us at the giving of the Torah, rather than a human power. Awe and the other attributes follow each person’s capacity, but love is a gift from the Holy One, blessed be He; therefore everyone is equal in silver, which represents love. The inner point unfolds according to the vessel’s preparation: one is clothed in a fine garment, another in a coarse garment, but the essential point is equal in every person of Israel.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Sefas Emes gives a complementary explanation of why rich and poor contribute the same amount: the inner divine gift is equal even when its manifestation differs. Rav Tzadok’s richer and poorer spiritual recipients likewise remain within one complete structure, rather than adding or subtracting a degree according to their personal attainment.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 7 — “When they are bound in one aguda, even the chelbenah joins the levonah and gives a good fragrance… therefore the half-shekel, ten gerah, the letter yud.” Rav Tzadok there ties the half-shekel to this same image: it gathers each individual into the whole of Yisrael, where even what was flawed is repaired and contributes.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Chaim Vital, Etz Chaim, Gate 23, chapter 8 — “Daas therefore completes the ten sefiros in place of Keser. This concerns the external aspect; in the internal aspect, Keser is included among Zeir Anpin's ten sefiros. Thus do not wonder that we sometimes count Daas among the ten sefiros and sometimes Keser, for one concerns the external aspect and the other the internal aspect. The inner aspect of Daas—what it is and whence it is drawn—requires investigation, since it appears to be an additional sefirah. It is possible that this is the meaning of ‘not fewer than nine and not more than ten’: in the external aspect there are nine sefiros, so Daas is needed to complete them; in the internal aspect Daas would be beyond ten. Therefore it says ‘ten and not eleven,’ for the inner aspect of Daas consists only of the roots of the inner aspect of the six extremities. But what these roots are still needs to be known and requires investigation.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The alternating enumeration explains how Daas can “fill the place of Keser” without becoming an eleventh independent light. Etz Chaim distinguishes external and internal aspects, rather than subtracting Keser from reality. Rav Tzadok applies the same numerical boundary to two forms of religious apprehension: achieved knowledge must not be counted as an added light, while the crown's concealment must not reduce the count to nine. Etz Chaim expressly leaves its further account of Daas's inner roots for investigation; that qualification belongs to the cited source.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 19, 38b; Introduction, 12a; Kesubos 111b — “The union of Torah scholars is from Shabbos to Shabbos, to inherit that drop, which is Chochmah—the dew of Torah for their children. It was not for nothing that the Sages established: Whoever engages in the dew of Torah, the dew of Torah revives him.” The Introduction, 12a, likewise speaks of dew descending on one who guards Shabbos: “Dew to revive the dead,” followed by the same teaching about the dew of Torah. Kesubos 111b expounds “Your dew is a dew of lights”: “Whoever uses the light of Torah, the light of Torah revives him.” The Tikkunim’s wording is dew; the retrieved Bavli wording is light.
